weeks.region: Eden between the Tigris and Euphrates (Iraq); Babel = Babylon (Iraq); Ararat (Turkey/Armenia)
weeks.family: Adam → Seth → Noah. Noah's sons (Gen 10): Shem (Semitic peoples: Hebrews, Arameans, Arabs), Ham (Egypt, Cush, Canaan), Japheth (northern peoples).
weeks.gods: The tower of Babel recalls a ziggurat, Mesopotamia's temple-mountain.
weeks.summary: God creates a good world and humans in his image. Disobedience breaks that relationship, and evil grows until the flood and the tower of Babel. Job, whom tradition places in the patriarchs' era, asks why the righteous suffer.

weeks.region: Uz: probably southern Jordan or northwestern Saudi Arabia; Teman (Edom, Jordan)
weeks.family: Job and his friends; Eliphaz the Temanite (a descendant of Esau).
weeks.gods: Job 31:26-28 refuses to kiss his hand toward the sun and moon, a star worship common in Arabia and Mesopotamia.
weeks.summary: Job argues with his friends, who think all suffering is punishment. God answers from the storm without explaining why, but shows the world is larger than humans can grasp.

weeks.region: Ur (southern Iraq) → Haran (southeastern Turkey) → Canaan (Israel/West Bank) → Egypt; Sodom (Dead Sea)
weeks.family: Terah → Abraham, Nahor and Haran (Lot's father). Abraham + Hagar → Ishmael (ancestor of northern Arabian tribes, Gen 25:12-18). Abraham + Sarah → Isaac → Esau and Jacob. Lot → Moab and Ammon (Jordan).
weeks.gods: Joshua 24:2 says Terah "worshiped other gods." Ur and Haran were the great centers of the moon god nanna/Sin.
weeks.summary: God calls Abraham to leave Ur and promises him descendants, land and blessing for all nations. The promise is tested by years of waiting, Ishmael, Isaac and the command to sacrifice him.

weeks.region: Haran (Turkey), Canaan, Egypt (Goshen, Nile Delta); Edom (southern Jordan)
weeks.family: Jacob + Leah, Rachel and two servants → 12 sons = 12 tribes. Esau → Edom (Gen 36). Abraham + Keturah → Midian (northwestern Saudi Arabia). Joseph marries Asenath, daughter of the priest of On.
weeks.gods: Rachel steals Laban's teraphim (household idols, 31:19). Jacob orders the foreign gods removed (35:2). On = Heliopolis, city of the sun god Ra.
weeks.summary: Jacob, the crafty grandson, becomes Israel and has twelve sons. Joseph is sold by his brothers, rises to govern Egypt and saves his family from famine: what they meant for evil, God used for good.

weeks.region: Egypt → Midian (northwestern Saudi Arabia) → Sinai (Egypt; some place it in Arabia)
weeks.family: Amram and Jochebed → Moses, Aaron and Miriam. Moses marries Zipporah, daughter of Jethro, priest of Midian.
weeks.gods: The plagues are a judgment "on all the gods of Egypt" (12:12): the Nile, the sun (Ra) and Pharaoh as a god.
weeks.note: Traditional route; the exact path of the Exodus is debated.
weeks.summary: Jacob's descendants are slaves in Egypt. God calls Moses, sends the plagues and frees his people; at Sinai he gives them the Ten Commandments.

weeks.region: Sinai Peninsula
weeks.family: Moses, Aaron, Joshua; Bezalel (builder of the tabernacle).
weeks.gods: The golden calf (ch. 32) recalls Egypt's apis bull and the bull as a symbol of El and baal in Canaan.
weeks.summary: Laws for living as a free people and the design of the tabernacle, the tent where God would dwell among them. Before it is finished, the people worship a golden calf.

weeks.region: Sinai
weeks.family: Aaron and his sons (Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, Ithamar): the origin of the priesthood.
weeks.gods: 18:21 and 20:2-5 forbid giving children to molech. 17:7 forbids sacrifices to "goat demons" of the desert.
weeks.summary: Leviticus explains how a holy God can live among an imperfect people: sacrifices, purity, festivals and the Day of Atonement. It also forbids neighboring practices, such as giving children to molech.

weeks.region: Sinai → Wilderness of Paran → Kadesh (Sinai/Negev, Egypt–Israel border)
weeks.family: Census of the 12 tribes; the Levites; Korah's rebellion (a Levite, Moses' cousin).
weeks.summary: Israel organizes and leaves Sinai, but when the spies return from Canaan, the people are afraid and refuse to enter. That generation will wander for 40 years.

weeks.region: Edom and Moab (Jordan), Jordan River; Balaam came from the Euphrates (Syria/Turkey)
weeks.family: The Moabites descend from Lot and the Midianites from Abraham and Keturah. Balaam also appears in an inscription at Deir Alla (Jordan).
weeks.gods: baal of Peor (ch. 25); chemosh, god of Moab (21:29); the bronze serpent (ch. 21).
weeks.summary: A new generation approaches Canaan from the east. The king of Moab hires Balaam to curse them, but he can only bless; afterward, Israel falls into the worship of baal of Peor.

weeks.region: Plains of Moab (Jordan), across from Jericho
weeks.family: Moses says farewell to the people.
weeks.gods: Ch. 12: destroy altars, asherah poles (posts of the goddess asherah) and sacred stones. 4:19: do not worship the sun, moon or stars.
weeks.summary: Moses reviews the story and renews the covenant before he dies: love God with all your heart and do not follow the gods of the land you are about to enter.

weeks.region: Mount Nebo (Jordan)
weeks.family: Joshua succeeds Moses; Moses dies.
weeks.gods: 18:10 forbids making children pass through the fire and divination. 32:17: sacrifices to demons, "new gods."
weeks.summary: Moses sets life and death, blessing and curse, before the people and urges them to choose life. He climbs Mount Nebo, sees the promised land and dies.

weeks.region: Jericho, Ai, Shechem and Hebron (West Bank); land divided across Israel and Jordan
weeks.family: Joshua, Caleb, Rahab (a Canaanite, ancestor of David).
weeks.gods: 24:2,15: choose between the gods "beyond the River" (Mesopotamia), those of the Amorites, or God.
weeks.summary: Joshua leads Israel across the Jordan; Jericho falls and the land is divided among the tribes. At the end, Joshua challenges them: choose today whom you will serve.

weeks.region: Israel, Galilee, Gaza (Philistines), Dan (northern Israel)
weeks.family: Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson and Delilah.
weeks.gods: baal and the Ashtoreths (2:13); Gideon tears down baal's altar (ch. 6); dagon, Philistine god in Gaza (16:23); chemosh (11:24).
weeks.summary: Without a faithful leader, Israel repeats a cycle: it abandons God for baal, is oppressed, cries out, and God raises a judge to rescue them. Each round is worse than the last.

weeks.region: Moab (Jordan) → Bethlehem (West Bank); Shiloh; Ashdod (Israel)
weeks.family: Ruth (a Moabite) + Boaz → Obed → Jesse → David. Eli, Samuel, Saul (tribe of Benjamin).
weeks.gods: The ark topples dagon's statue in Ashdod (ch. 5); the Baals and Ashtoreths are put away (7:4).
weeks.summary: Ruth, a foreigner from Moab, shows a faithfulness missing in Israel and becomes David's great-grandmother. Samuel is born in answer to prayer, and the people ask for a king: Saul.

weeks.region: Bethlehem, Valley of Elah, Gath (Philistines), Endor, Beth-shan (Israel)
weeks.family: David (son of Jesse, tribe of Judah); Jonathan; Michal, Saul's daughter and David's wife; Goliath of Gath.
weeks.gods: Saul consults the medium of Endor; his armor ends up in the temple of the Ashtoreths (31:10).
weeks.summary: Saul disobeys and God chooses David, a young shepherd. David defeats Goliath and spends years fleeing a jealous Saul without taking revenge.

weeks.region: Hebron, Jerusalem (taken from the Jebusites), Rabbah of Ammon = Amman, capital of Jordan
weeks.family: David, Bathsheba, Uriah the Hittite, the prophet Nathan.
weeks.gods: David burns the Philistine idols (5:21) and takes the crown of milcom, the Ammonite god (12:30).
weeks.summary: David becomes king, takes Jerusalem and receives a promise: his dynasty will last forever. Then he commits adultery with Bathsheba and has Uriah killed.

weeks.region: Jerusalem; Geshur (Golan Heights/Syria)
weeks.family: Absalom (son of David and Maacah of Geshur), Amnon, Tamar, Joab.
weeks.gods: Psalm 16:4: those who run after other gods multiply their sorrows.
weeks.summary: The consequences of David's sin reach his family: violence among his sons and Absalom's rebellion. The psalms show David praying through it all.

weeks.region: All Israel
weeks.family: Complete genealogies: from Adam to Abraham, the 12 tribes and the house of David.
weeks.gods: Saul's head in the temple of dagon (10:10); the tribes east of the Jordan follow foreign gods (5:25).
weeks.summary: Chronicles retells the story from Adam to David, written for those who returned from exile: it reminds them who they are and highlights the temple and worship.

weeks.region: Jerusalem (Zion)
weeks.family: David, the sons of Korah, Asaph.
weeks.gods: Psalm 29 resembles hymns from Ugarit (Syria) to the storm god baal, but credits the storm to God.
weeks.summary: The Psalms are Israel's prayer book: praise, lament, trust and protest. Many are David's and use images their neighbors applied to baal, but directed to God.

weeks.region: Jerusalem
weeks.family: David (Psalm 51 follows the Bathsheba affair), Asaph.
weeks.gods: Psalm 68:4: "him who rides on the clouds," a title of baal at Ugarit, applied to God.
weeks.summary: More psalms of David and Asaph, including Psalm 51, the prayer of repentance after the Bathsheba affair.

weeks.region: Jerusalem
weeks.family: Asaph; Moses (Psalm 90).
weeks.gods: Psalm 82: God judges among the "gods." 96:5: the gods of the nations are idols.
weeks.summary: Psalms about Israel's history and about God as king of all the earth, above the gods of the nations.

weeks.region: Jerusalem
weeks.family: David.
weeks.gods: Psalm 106:28, 37-38: baal of Peor and children sacrificed to the idols of Canaan. 115: idols that cannot see or hear.
weeks.summary: Psalms of praise and remembrance: they recall Israel's failures in the wilderness and the folly of idols that cannot see or hear.

weeks.region: Jerusalem; Babylon (Iraq) in Psalm 137
weeks.family: David; the exiles.
weeks.gods: Psalm 135:15-18: idols of silver and gold.
weeks.summary: The last psalms: songs of pilgrimage to Jerusalem, the lament of exile in Babylon, and a great closing of praise.

weeks.region: Jerusalem; Tyre (Lebanon); Sheba (Yemen, perhaps also Ethiopia); Ophir (uncertain)
weeks.family: Solomon (son of David and Bathsheba); Hiram, king of Tyre; the queen of Sheba; foreign wives.
weeks.gods: 11:5-7: Solomon builds altars to ashtoreth, milcom, chemosh and molech.
weeks.summary: Solomon receives wisdom, builds the temple and brings Israel to its peak of wealth. But his foreign wives lead him to build altars to other gods.

weeks.region: Jerusalem; Massa (northern Arabia)
weeks.family: Solomon; Agur and King Lemuel (chs. 30-31), perhaps from Massa, an Ishmaelite tribe (Gen 25:14).
weeks.summary: Proverbs teaches practical wisdom for work, money, words and relationships: the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom.

weeks.region: Jerusalem; Lebanon, Gilead (Jordan)
weeks.family: Solomon.
weeks.summary: Ecclesiastes asks what anything means under the sun, and the Song of Songs celebrates love between a man and a woman.

weeks.region: Northern Israel (Samaria), Judah (Jerusalem); Mount Carmel (Haifa); Sidon (Lebanon); Damascus (Syria)
weeks.family: Rehoboam (son of Solomon) against Jeroboam. Ahab + Jezebel, daughter of Ethbaal, king of Sidon. The prophet Elijah.
weeks.gods: Golden calves at Dan and Bethel; Jezebel imposes baal and asherah; Elijah against 450 prophets of baal on Carmel (1 Kgs 18).
weeks.summary: The kingdom splits into Israel (north) and Judah (south). Jeroboam sets up golden calves, and Ahab and Jezebel impose baal; Elijah confronts them on Mount Carmel.

weeks.region: Samaria; Ekron (Israel); Moab (Jordan); Damascus; Nineveh = Mosul (Iraq)
weeks.family: Elisha; Jehu; Athaliah (Jezebel's daughter, queen of Judah); Joash; Jonah.
weeks.gods: baal-zebub of Ekron (2 Kgs 1); the king of Moab sacrifices his son (3:27); Jehu destroys baal's temple (ch. 10); Rimmon, Syrian god (5:18).
weeks.summary: Elisha continues Elijah's work with miracles; Jehu wipes out Ahab's house and baal's temple. Jonah is sent to Nineveh, the enemy capital, which repents.

weeks.region: Northern Israel (Bethel, Samaria); Tekoa (West Bank)
weeks.family: Amos (a shepherd from Tekoa); Hosea and Gomer (his marriage as a symbol).
weeks.gods: Hosea 2: Israel credits baal for its harvests; the calf of Samaria (8:5). Amos 5:26: the astral gods Sikkuth and Kiyyun.
weeks.summary: Israel enjoys a prosperous but unjust era. Amos denounces the oppression of the poor, and Hosea compares Israel's idolatry to a betrayed marriage.

weeks.region: Assyria (northern Iraq) conquers Samaria in 722 BC; Judah
weeks.family: Kings Uzziah, Jotham and Ahaz; Isaiah; Micah.
weeks.gods: Ahaz makes his son pass through the fire (2 Kgs 16:3). 2 Kgs 17:29-31: settlers bring Nergal, Adrammelech and other gods, with child sacrifice.
weeks.summary: Assyria rises and in 722 BC destroys Samaria: the northern kingdom vanishes after two centuries of warnings. In Judah, Isaiah and Micah announce judgment and a future king from David's line.

weeks.region: Assyria, Babylon, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, Tyre, Edom, Cush (Sudan); Dedan and Tema = AlUla and Tayma (Saudi Arabia, Isa 21:13-14)
weeks.family: Isaiah.
weeks.gods: 14:12: "morning star, son of the dawn" (Shahar was the Canaanite god of dawn); asherah poles (17:8); idols of Egypt (ch. 19); chemosh (16:12).
weeks.summary: Isaiah speaks to the neighboring nations: Assyria, Babylon, Moab, Egypt and Arabia. No empire is eternal; only God rules history.

weeks.region: Jerusalem besieged by Sennacherib (Assyria, Iraq); Lachish (Israel)
weeks.family: Hezekiah (son of Ahaz); Isaiah; Sennacherib.
weeks.gods: Hezekiah destroys the bronze serpent people worshiped (2 Kgs 18:4); Nisroch, Sennacherib's god; Bel and Nebo = marduk and nabu, gods of Babylon (Isa 46:1).
weeks.summary: King Hezekiah purifies the temple. Sennacherib of Assyria besieges Jerusalem, but the city is spared. Isaiah announces comfort and mocks the making of idols.

weeks.region: Babylon (Iraq), Nineveh (Mosul, Iraq); Midian, Sheba, Kedar and Nebaioth (Arabia, Isa 60:6-7)
weeks.family: Kedar and Nebaioth were sons of Ishmael; Nahum.
weeks.gods: Isa 57:5-9: child sacrifice in the valleys. 65:11: Gad and meni, gods of fortune (some link meni to the Arabian goddess manat).
weeks.summary: Isaiah describes the suffering servant and the future restoration of Jerusalem for all nations. Nahum announces the fall of Nineveh.

weeks.region: Jerusalem destroyed by Babylon (586 BC); Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom (Jerusalem)
weeks.family: Manasseh, Amon, Josiah (the reformer), Zedekiah; Nebuchadnezzar.
weeks.gods: Manasseh: baal, asherah, star worship and the sacrifice of his son. Josiah destroys Topheth, the horses of the sun and the altars of chemosh, milcom and ashtoreth (2 Kgs 23).
weeks.summary: Manasseh fills Judah with idols and sacrifices his son; Josiah finds the Book of the Law and leads a great reform. But it is too late: Babylon destroys Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BC.

weeks.region: Jerusalem, Anathoth (West Bank)
weeks.family: Jeremiah (son of a priest from Anathoth).
weeks.gods: 2:28: as many gods as towns. 7:18: the "Queen of Heaven" (probably astarte/ishtar). 19:5: children burned to baal.
weeks.summary: Jeremiah, a young prophet, warns for decades that Judah will fall unless it abandons baal and the Queen of Heaven. He is persecuted and imprisoned.

weeks.region: Jerusalem under siege; Babylon
weeks.family: Baruch (Jeremiah's scribe), Zedekiah, the Rechabites.
weeks.gods: 32:35: high places of baal in Hinnom to make children pass through the fire to molech.
weeks.summary: During Babylon's siege, Jeremiah buys a field as a sign of hope and announces a new covenant written on the heart.

weeks.region: Egypt (Tahpanhes, Memphis); Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus; Kedar (Arabia, 49:28)
weeks.family: Jeremiah is taken to Egypt; Gedaliah.
weeks.gods: Ch. 44: Judeans in Egypt return to the Queen of Heaven; Amon of Thebes (46:25); chemosh; milcom; Bel and Merodach = marduk (50:2).
weeks.summary: Jerusalem falls. A group flees to Egypt, taking Jeremiah, and returns to idolatry. Lamentations mourns the ruined city but affirms that God's mercies are new every morning.

weeks.region: Babylon; Kebar River (southern Iraq, near Nippur)
weeks.family: Ezekiel (an exiled priest).
weeks.gods: Ch. 8: women weeping for tammuz (a Mesopotamian god) in the temple; men worshiping the sun toward the east.
weeks.summary: Ezekiel, deported to Babylon, sees God's glory leave the temple because of the idolatry practiced inside, even the worship of tammuz and the sun.

weeks.region: Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre and Sidon (Lebanon), Egypt; Arabia and Kedar (27:21)
weeks.family: Ezekiel; the king of Tyre.
weeks.gods: The king of Tyre says "I am a god" (28:2); idols of Memphis (30:13).
weeks.summary: Ezekiel announces judgment on the nations and then hope: dry bones that come back to life and a new temple where God dwells again.

weeks.region: Babylon (Iraq), Susa (Iran), Edom (Jordan), Jerusalem
weeks.family: Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego; Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, Cyrus (Persia), Zerubbabel. Obadiah: Edom = Esau.
weeks.gods: Nebuchadnezzar's golden statue (Dan 3); Bel = marduk; Belshazzar toasts gods of gold with the temple vessels (Dan 5).
weeks.summary: Daniel and his friends stay faithful in Babylon's court. Persia conquers Babylon, and Cyrus lets the Jews return and rebuild the temple.

weeks.region: Jerusalem; Susa (Iran)
weeks.family: Zerubbabel, Joshua the high priest; Esther and Mordecai (Benjamites), Haman, Ahasuerus (Xerxes I).
weeks.gods: Zech 10:2: teraphim; 13:2: removing the names of the idols. Esther never mentions God.
weeks.summary: Haggai and Zechariah urge the people to finish the temple. In Persia, Esther risks her life to save her people from a plot of extermination.

weeks.region: Jerusalem; Persia (Iran); northern Arabia (Geshem)
weeks.family: Ezra (scribe), Nehemiah (cupbearer to Artaxerxes), Sanballat, Tobiah the Ammonite, Geshem the Arab (Neh 2:19).
weeks.gods: Mal 2:11: marrying "the daughter of a foreign god."
weeks.summary: Ezra teaches the Law and Nehemiah rebuilds Jerusalem's walls. Malachi, the last prophet, rebukes lukewarm faith and announces a messenger to come.

weeks.region: Bethlehem, Nazareth, Galilee (northern Israel), Egypt, Jerusalem, Caesarea Philippi (Golan Heights)
weeks.family: Genealogy of Jesus (ch. 1): from Abraham to David to Joseph, including Tamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bathsheba; the Magi from the east.
weeks.gods: Beelzebul (12:24) comes from baal-zebub; Caesarea Philippi had a shrine to the Greek god Pan (16:13).
weeks.summary: After 400 years of prophetic silence, Jesus is born. Matthew presents him as the Messiah, son of David, who fulfills the promises through his teaching, death and resurrection.

weeks.region: Galilee; Decapolis (Gerasa = Jerash, Jordan); Tyre and Sidon (Lebanon)
weeks.family: John the Baptist (son of Zechariah and Elizabeth, Mary's relative); the Twelve.
weeks.gods: The Decapolis were Greek cities with temples to zeus and artemis; Beelzebul (Mark 3:22).
weeks.summary: Mark tells Jesus' life quickly and directly; Luke begins with his birth and his concern for the poor, women and outcasts.

weeks.region: Samaria, Jerusalem, Bethany, Jericho (West Bank)
weeks.family: Martha, Mary and Lazarus; Zacchaeus; Herod Antipas; the Samaritan woman.
weeks.gods: John 4: the Samaritans, descendants of the settlers of 2 Kgs 17, worshiped on Mount Gerizim.
weeks.summary: Luke follows Jesus' journey to Jerusalem with parables like the prodigal son. John presents Jesus as the Word made flesh.

weeks.region: Jerusalem, Samaria, Gaza, Damascus (Syria), Antioch (Antakya, Turkey)
weeks.family: Peter, Stephen, Saul/Paul (from Tarsus, Turkey), Cornelius, Herod Agrippa I.
weeks.gods: Simon the sorcerer (Acts 8); Herod accepts being hailed as a god (12:22).
weeks.summary: John tells of the Last Supper, the death and the resurrection. In Acts, the Holy Spirit comes and the church grows from Jerusalem to Samaria and to non-Jews.

weeks.region: Cyprus; Turkey (Galatia, Lystra); Greece (Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth)
weeks.family: Paul, Barnabas, Silas, Timothy, Lydia, Priscilla and Aquila; James, the brother of Jesus.
weeks.gods: In Lystra they think Paul and Barnabas are hermes and zeus (Acts 14); in Athens, "to an unknown god" (ch. 17).
weeks.note: Approximate route of Paul's first and second journeys.
weeks.summary: Paul and Barnabas take the message to Cyprus, Turkey and Greece. Their first letters teach that salvation is by grace, not by keeping the Law.

weeks.region: Corinth (Greece)
weeks.family: Paul, Apollos, Peter (Cephas).
weeks.gods: Food sacrificed to idols (1 Cor 8 and 10); Corinth had a great temple of Aphrodite.
weeks.summary: Paul writes to the church in Corinth, a city of pagan temples, about divisions, food offered to idols, love and the resurrection.

weeks.region: Rome (Italy), Ephesus (Turkey), Malta, Caesarea
weeks.family: Paul, Phoebe, Felix, Festus, Agrippa II, Luke.
weeks.gods: Ephesus: artemis/Diana, whose temple was one of the Seven Wonders (Acts 19); in Malta they think Paul is a god (28:6).
weeks.note: Rome and Malta are off the map, to the west.
weeks.summary: Romans explains the gospel in an orderly way. In Ephesus there is a riot over the worship of artemis; Paul is arrested in Jerusalem and reaches Rome as a prisoner.

weeks.reading: Ephesians; Philippians; Colossians; Philemon; 1 Timothy; Titus; 1 Peter
weeks.region: Turkey (Ephesus, Colossae), Greece (Philippi), Crete, Rome
weeks.family: Paul, Timothy, Titus, Onesimus and Philemon, Peter, Silvanus.
weeks.gods: Col 2:18: worship of angels; Eph 6:12: spiritual powers.
weeks.note: Rome is off the map, to the west.
weeks.summary: Letters written from prison and to church leaders: unity in Christ, joy in suffering and how to organize the church.

weeks.reading: 2 Timothy; 2 Peter; Hebrews; Jude; 1 John; 2 John; 3 John
weeks.region: Rome; Asia Minor (Turkey)
weeks.family: Timothy (his mother Eunice and grandmother Lois), Jude (brother of James), John.
weeks.gods: 1 John 5:21: "keep yourselves from idols"; Jude 11: Balaam and Korah.
weeks.note: Rome is off the map, to the west.
weeks.summary: The last letters of Paul and Peter, Hebrews, which shows Jesus as greater than Moses and the temple, and the warnings of Jude and John against false teachers.

weeks.region: Patmos (Greece); 7 churches in western Turkey (Ephesus, Smyrna = Izmir, Pergamum = Bergama, etc.); "Babylon" as a symbol of Rome
weeks.family: John; "Jezebel" and "Balaam" as symbolic names for false teachers.
weeks.gods: "Satan's throne" in Pergamum (the great altar of zeus or the emperor cult); worship of the beast (ch. 13).
weeks.summary: John, exiled on Patmos under pressure from the emperor cult, sees visions of God's throne, the fall of "Babylon" and a new heaven and new earth.

gods.name: baal
gods.region: Lebanon, Syria, Israel and Jordan; his great textual center is Ugarit (Syria).
gods.what: His name means "lord" or "owner." He was the god of storm and rain, on whom the harvests depended. He had many local forms: baal of Peor (Moab) and baal-zebub of Ekron, the source of "Beelzebul" in the Gospels.
gods.bible: Judges 6, 1 Kings 18 (Elijah on Carmel), Hosea 2, Jeremiah 19:5.
gods.today: His worship disappeared in antiquity. Today only small neopagan groups that try to reconstruct Canaanite religion honor him. Some scholars propose that the name of the Arabian god hubal comes from baal, but it is a debated hypothesis (see hubal).

gods.name: asherah
gods.what: Mother goddess, consort of the god El at Ugarit. She was worshiped with wooden poles or trees called "Asherahs." An inscription at Kuntillet Ajrud (Sinai) reads "Yahweh and his asherah," evidence that some Israelites mixed the cults, which is exactly what the prophets denounce.
gods.today: There is no continuous worship. She appears in some modern neopagan practices.

gods.name: astarte / queen of heaven
gods.region: Lebanon (Sidon), Israel, Iraq (as ishtar) and Egypt.
gods.what: Goddess of love, fertility and war; in the Bible she appears as Ashtaroth or ashtoreth. She corresponds to the Mesopotamian ishtar and was later assimilated to the Greek Aphrodite. Jeremiah's "Queen of Heaven" is probably her: people baked cakes and poured out drink offerings to her.
gods.today: Her ancient worship ended. Her figure is used today in Wicca and other neopagan movements.

gods.name: molech
gods.region: Amman (Jordan) and the Valley of Hinnom in Jerusalem.
gods.what: Associated with child sacrifice, "passing through the fire," at the Topheth of Jerusalem. Scholars debate whether molech was a god or the name of a type of sacrifice (molk), like the one found in the tophets of Carthage. The famous image of a bull-headed statue with burning arms comes from medieval rabbinic descriptions and 19th-century engravings, not from archaeology.
gods.today: There is no worship. molech is used mostly as a symbol in popular culture and social criticism.

gods.name: chemosh
gods.region: Central Jordan, east of the Dead Sea.
gods.what: National god of Moab, the people descended from Lot. The Mesha Stele (c. 840 BC, now in the Louvre) is an inscription by the Moabite king Mesha crediting chemosh with his victories over Israel: the other side of 2 Kings 3.
gods.today: Disappeared along with the Moabite people.

gods.name: milcom
gods.region: Amman, capital of Jordan (ancient Rabbah of Ammon).
gods.what: Chief god of the Ammonites, descendants of Lot. His name comes from the root for "king." David took his crown at Rabbah.

gods.name: dagon
gods.region: Gaza and Ashdod (Israel/Gaza); earlier Mari and Ugarit (Syria).
gods.what: God of grain and fertility. The idea that he was a "fish god" is a later interpretation without good support.
gods.today: No worship. Today he appears mostly in fiction (for example, in H. P. Lovecraft).

gods.name: marduk (bel) and nabu (nebo)
gods.what: marduk, called Bel ("lord"), was the chief god of Babylon; nabu was his son, god of writing. Nebuchadnezzar's name contains nabu.
gods.today: Small groups reconstruct Mesopotamian religion, but there is no continuous worship.

gods.name: tammuz
gods.what: Dumuzi in Sumerian: a shepherd god who died and was mourned every summer. Ezekiel sees women weeping for him in the very temple of Jerusalem.
gods.today: His name lives on in the calendar: tammuz is a month of the Hebrew calendar and, in Levantine and Iraqi Arabic, the name for July.

gods.name: sin (nanna) and star worship
gods.region: Ur (southern Iraq) and Haran (southeastern Turkey); also Tayma (Saudi Arabia).
gods.what: The moon god had his great temples at Ur and Haran, the two cities of Abraham's family. The last king of Babylon, Nabonidus, lived ten years in Tayma in Arabia and was devoted to Sin. The Bible repeatedly forbids worshiping the sun, moon and stars.
gods.today: In Haran, pagan groups kept worshiping the stars until around the 11th century AD. No worship remains today.

gods.name: gods of Egypt
gods.what: Ra (the sun), Amun of Thebes, the apis bull, the deified Nile (Hapi) and Pharaoh as son of the gods. The plagues of the Exodus are presented as a judgment on them.
gods.today: Kemetism is a modern movement that reconstructs Egyptian religion. There has been no continuous worship since antiquity.

gods.name: Greek and Roman gods
gods.region: Greece and Turkey (Ephesus, Pergamum, Lystra), Golan Heights (Pan).
gods.what: zeus, hermes, artemis (Diana), Aphrodite, Pan, Castor and Pollux, and the cult of the Roman emperor. They are the backdrop of Acts, the letters and Revelation.
gods.today: Greece legally recognized Hellenic religion in 2017, and there are modern groups that practice it.

gods.name: gad and meni
gods.what: Gods of fortune and destiny to whom tables and drinks were offered. Some researchers link meni to manat, the Arabian goddess of destiny; the Quran mentions manat with al-Lat and al-Uzza as pre-Islamic goddesses (Quran 53:19-20).
gods.today: No worship. manat and the other goddesses were rejected by Islam.

gods.name: hubal (Arabian context, not in the Bible)
gods.region: Mecca (Saudi Arabia); his name seems to come from the north, the Nabataean area (Jordan, northwestern Arabia).
gods.what: His statue was the main idol of the Kaaba before Islam, among some 360 idols. One hypothesis reads his name as "hu-bal," "he is baal," but the evidence is thin and debated. The Bible does not mention him; what does appear in your reading are the peoples of that region: Ishmael, Kedar, Nebaioth, Tema and Dedan.
gods.bible: Does not appear. Context: Genesis 25:12-18, Isaiah 21:13-17, 60:7.
gods.today: In AD 630, when Muhammad took Mecca, the statue of hubal and the other idols were destroyed, and Islam regards him as a false idol. The idea that Allah is hubal or a moon god (Winckler in 1901, popularized by pastor Robert Morey in the 1990s) is rejected by historians. Patricia Crone notes that if they were the same god, "hubal" would have survived as a name of Allah, and it did not. Arab Christians also call God "Allah."

eras.name: Creation and fall
eras.summary: God creates the world and humanity; sin breaks the relationship. The flood and Babel.

eras.name: Patriarchs
eras.summary: God promises Abraham a family, a land, and blessing for all nations through him.

eras.name: Exodus and wilderness
eras.summary: Israel leaves Egypt, receives the Law at Sinai and spends 40 years in the wilderness.

eras.name: Conquest and judges
eras.summary: Entry into Canaan and cycles of unfaithfulness, oppression and rescue.

eras.name: United kingdom
eras.summary: Saul, David and Solomon. The promise of an eternal kingdom to David and the building of the temple.

eras.name: Divided kingdom
eras.summary: The kingdom splits into Israel and Judah. Prophets warn for centuries before the exile.

eras.name: Exile and return
eras.summary: Babylon destroys Jerusalem; decades later the people return and rebuild.

eras.name: Jesus
eras.summary: The life, teaching, death and resurrection of Jesus.

eras.name: The church
eras.summary: The message spreads from Jerusalem to Rome; the letters and Revelation.

tree.name: Adam and Eve
tree.note: The first humans, created in God's image.

children.name: Seth
children.note: Born after Abel's death; the story continues through his line (Gen 4–5).

children.name: Noah
children.note: Ten generations after Adam. He survives the flood, and his three sons give rise to the nations (Gen 10).

children.name: Shem
children.note: Ancestor of Hebrews, Arameans, Assyrians and Arabs.

children.name: Terah
children.note: Nine generations after Shem. He lived in Ur and "worshiped other gods" (Josh 24:2).

children.name: Abraham
children.note: God calls him to leave Ur and promises him descendants, land and blessing for all nations.

children.name: Ishmael
children.note: Son of Abraham and Hagar, the Egyptian servant. God promises to make him a great nation.

children.name: Nebaioth, Kedar, Tema…
children.note: His twelve sons give their names to tribes of Saudi Arabia and Jordan. Islamic tradition sees Ishmael as ancestor of the northern Arabs.

children.name: Isaac
children.note: Son of the promise, of Abraham and Sarah. He marries Rebekah, Nahor's granddaughter.

children.name: Esau
children.note: Jacob's older twin; he sells his birthright. Father of the Edomites.

children.name: Jacob (Israel)
children.note: With Leah, Rachel, Bilhah and Zilpah he has twelve sons: the tribes of Israel.

children.name: Levi
children.note: His tribe is set apart to serve at the tabernacle and temple.

children.name: Moses, Aaron and Miriam
children.note: Children of Amram and Jochebed. Moses leads the Exodus; Aaron is the first high priest.

children.name: Judah
children.note: The kings will come from his tribe; Jacob promises him the scepter (Gen 49:10).

children.name: Perez
children.note: Son of Judah and Tamar (Gen 38).

children.name: Boaz and Ruth
children.note: A faithful foreigner joins the Messiah's family.

children.name: David
children.note: Ruth's great-grandson. God promises him an eternal kingdom (2 Sam 7).

children.name: Solomon
children.note: Son of David and Bathsheba; he builds the temple.

children.name: Kings of Judah
children.note: From Rehoboam to Zedekiah, until the exile in Babylon.

children.name: Joseph, Mary and Jesus
children.note: Matthew 1 follows David's line to Joseph, husband of Mary.

children.name: Benjamin
children.note: Jacob's youngest, Rachel's son.

children.name: Saul, Esther and Paul
children.note: This tribe produced the first king, Queen Esther and the apostle Paul.

children.name: Joseph
children.note: Sold into Egypt, he rises to govern; his sons head two northern tribes.

children.name: Midian
children.note: Son of Abraham and Keturah; father of the Midianites.

children.name: Jethro and Zipporah
children.note: Jethro, priest of Midian; his daughter Zipporah marries Moses.

children.name: Nahor
children.note: Abraham's brother.

children.name: Rebekah and Laban
children.note: Nahor's grandchildren. Rebekah marries Isaac; Laban's daughters, Leah and Rachel, marry Jacob.

children.name: Lot
children.note: Abraham's nephew, son of Haran. He escapes Sodom.

children.name: Moab
children.note: Father of the Moabites, the people of Ruth and of the false god chemosh.

children.name: Ben-ammi
children.note: Father of the Ammonites, the people of the false god milcom.

children.name: Ham
children.note: Father of Cush (Sudan/Ethiopia), Mizraim (Egypt), Put (Libya) and Canaan (Canaanites and Phoenicians).

children.name: Japheth
children.note: Father of Javan (Greeks), Gomer, Magog and other peoples of Anatolia and beyond.

extras.name: Tobit
extras.what: Story of a devout Jewish family exiled in Nineveh; the angel Raphael guides young Tobias on his journey.
extras.rel: Set in the Assyrian exile you read in 2 Kings 17; shows how deported Israelites lived out their faith.
extras.canon: Catholic and Orthodox; apocryphal for Protestants and Jews.

extras.name: Judith
extras.what: A Jewish widow saves her people by defeating the general Holofernes, sent by "Nebuchadnezzar."
extras.rel: It deliberately mixes figures from different eras; it reads as an exemplary tale rather than a chronicle.

extras.name: Wisdom of Solomon
extras.what: Written in Greek in Alexandria; praises divine wisdom and sharply criticizes idolatry.
extras.rel: Chapters 13–15 explain the origin of idols, useful alongside Isaiah 44 and Jeremiah 10.

extras.name: Sirach (Ecclesiasticus)
extras.what: Proverbs of Jesus ben Sira, a Jerusalem teacher; his grandson translated it into Greek.
extras.rel: Continues the style of Proverbs; chapters 44–50 review Israel's great figures.
extras.canon: Catholic and Orthodox; Hebrew fragments were found at Masada and Qumran.

extras.name: Baruch and Letter of Jeremiah
extras.what: Attributed to Jeremiah's scribe; includes a letter mocking the idols of Babylon.
extras.rel: Pairs with Jeremiah 36–45 and Lamentations; the letter describes the Babylonian cult the exiles faced.

extras.name: 1 and 2 Maccabees
extras.what: The Jewish revolt against Antiochus IV, who defiled the temple with an altar to zeus (167 BC), and the temple's rededication.
extras.rel: Fills the "400 silent years" between Malachi and Matthew; explains the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) in John 10:22.
extras.canon: Catholic and Orthodox; historical for Jews and Protestants.

extras.name: Additions to Daniel and Esther
extras.what: Susanna, Bel and the Dragon, the Prayer of Azariah, and Greek verses added to Esther that do mention God.
extras.rel: "Bel and the Dragon" shows Daniel unmasking the priests of Bel (marduk) in Babylon.

extras.name: Prayer of Manasseh
extras.what: A prayer of repentance attributed to King Manasseh in captivity.
extras.rel: Expands 2 Chronicles 33:12-13, where Manasseh humbles himself before God.

extras.name: 1 Enoch
extras.what: Visions attributed to Enoch; its "Book of the Watchers" expands Genesis 6: angels who unite with women and teach forbidden secrets.
extras.rel: Jude 14-15 quotes it directly, and 2 Peter 2:4 alludes to it. Widely read in Jesus' time: copies were found at Qumran.
extras.canon: Canonical only in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.

extras.name: Jubilees
extras.what: Retells Genesis and part of Exodus in 49-year periods; adds details such as Abraham's youth.
extras.rel: Tells how Abraham burned his father Terah's house of idols, expanding Joshua 24:2.
extras.canon: Canonical in the Ethiopian Church; copies at Qumran.

extras.name: Apocalypse of Abraham
extras.what: Abraham discovers that the wood and stone idols his father makes cannot even save themselves.
extras.rel: Portrays the idolatrous setting of Ur that the Bible barely mentions; a similar tradition appears in Jewish midrash and the Quran.

extras.name: Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs
extras.what: The last words of each son of Jacob to his descendants, with moral advice.
extras.rel: Expands Genesis 49 and the Joseph story; helps you see each tribe as a person.
extras.canon: Non-canonical; included in some Armenian Bibles.

extras.name: Martyrdom and Ascension of Isaiah
extras.what: Tells how King Manasseh had the prophet Isaiah sawn in two.
extras.rel: Hebrews 11:37 ("they were sawn in two") probably alludes to this tradition; it ties to the persecuted prophets.

extras.name: 2 Esdras (4 Ezra)
extras.what: Visions of "Ezra" asking why God allowed Jerusalem's destruction.
extras.rel: Written after the temple fell in AD 70, but set in the Babylonian exile.
extras.canon: Appendix of the Vulgate; canonical in some Eastern churches.

extras.name: Psalms of Solomon
extras.what: Eighteen psalms written after the Roman conquest of Jerusalem (63 BC).
extras.rel: Psalm 17 describes the Messiah, son of David, expected in Jesus' time.
extras.canon: Non-canonical; appears in some Greek manuscripts.

extras.name: Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ)
extras.what: A complete copy of Isaiah found in 1947 in Qumran Cave 1; displayed at the Shrine of the Book in Jerusalem.
extras.rel: It is about a thousand years older than the medieval Hebrew manuscripts and agrees with them in substance.
extras.canon: A manuscript of the canonical book of Isaiah.

extras.name: Genesis Apocryphon
extras.what: An Aramaic retelling of Genesis with first-person stories of Lamech, Noah and Abraham.
extras.rel: Describes Sarah's beauty and Abraham's dream before entering Egypt (Genesis 12).

extras.name: 4QSamuelᵃ
extras.what: A copy of Samuel with readings that sometimes match the Greek Septuagint.
extras.rel: Gives Goliath "four cubits and a span" (about 2 m) instead of six cubits, and includes a paragraph about Nahash the Ammonite before 1 Samuel 11.
extras.canon: A manuscript of the canonical book of Samuel.

extras.name: Habakkuk Pesher
extras.what: A commentary applying Habakkuk 1–2 to the Qumran community and its "Teacher of Righteousness."
extras.rel: Shows how the prophets were read in Jesus' time: as messages for their own day.

extras.name: Psalm 151 (11QPsᵃ)
extras.what: A psalm about young David, the anointed shepherd who defeats Goliath; it appears in the Psalms scroll from Cave 11.
extras.rel: The Orthodox Bible includes it at the end of Psalms.

extras.name: Community Rule and War Scroll
extras.what: The Qumran community's rules of life and a final battle between the "sons of light" and the "sons of darkness."
extras.rel: The language of light and darkness recalls John's Gospel; the final battle recalls Revelation.

extras.name: Epic of Gilgamesh
extras.what: Mesopotamian poem; in tablet XI, Utnapishtim survives a flood in a boat and sends out birds to find land.
extras.rel: A close parallel to Noah (Genesis 6–9); the differences in the flood's motive and the picture of God are telling.

extras.name: Enuma Elish
extras.what: Babylonian creation myth: marduk defeats the chaos goddess Tiamat and forms the world from her body.
extras.rel: Contrasts with Genesis 1, where creation happens by the word of one God, with no battle among gods.

extras.name: baal Cycle (Ugarit)
extras.what: Poems found at Ras Shamra (Syria) about baal, the storm god, and his fight against Yam (sea) and Mot (death).
extras.rel: Explains why Elijah challenges baal with fire and rain on Carmel, and why Psalms 29 and 68 use his titles for God.

extras.name: Merneptah Stele
extras.what: Inscription of Pharaoh Merneptah boasting of victories in Canaan: "Israel is laid waste."
extras.rel: It is the oldest known mention of Israel outside the Bible, in the period of the judges.

extras.name: Mesha Stele
extras.what: King Mesha of Moab tells of his revolt against Israel, credited to the god chemosh.
extras.rel: The other side of 2 Kings 3; it mentions Omri, king of Israel, and the name YHWH.

extras.name: Tel Dan Stele
extras.what: An Aramaic inscription by a king of Damascus mentioning the "house of David."
extras.rel: The first mention of David outside the Bible; fits Jehu's war in 2 Kings 9–10.

extras.name: Deir Alla Inscription
extras.what: A plaster text from a building in Jordan about "Balaam son of Beor, seer of the gods."
extras.rel: The same Balaam of Numbers 22–24, remembered outside Israel centuries later.

extras.name: Sennacherib's Prism and Lachish reliefs
extras.what: The Assyrian king boasts of shutting up Hezekiah in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage"; the Nineveh reliefs show the siege of Lachish.
extras.rel: The Assyrian side of 2 Kings 18–19 and Isaiah 36–37: it does not claim to have taken Jerusalem.

extras.name: Lachish letters
extras.what: Messages on pottery from a Judean officer as Babylon advanced on Judah.
extras.rel: One says the signals of Azekah can no longer be seen, as in Jeremiah 34:7.

extras.name: Babylonian Chronicles
extras.what: Tablets recording, year by year, the campaigns of the Babylonian kings.
extras.rel: They date Nebuchadnezzar's capture of Jerusalem to March 16, 597 BC (2 Kings 24:10-17).

extras.name: Cyrus Cylinder
extras.what: Cyrus of Persia announces that he returned deported peoples to their lands and restored their shrines.
extras.rel: Matches the policy of Ezra 1 and Isaiah 45, which calls Cyrus "anointed."

extras.name: Elephantine papyri
extras.what: Letters from a Jewish colony in Egypt that had its own temple to "Yahu" and asked Jerusalem for help rebuilding it.
extras.rel: Some of their names also honor Anat, echoing the mixing of cults Jeremiah 44 denounces among the Jews in Egypt.

extras.name: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews
extras.what: A history of the Jewish people written in Greek by a Jewish priest who lived through the war with Rome.
extras.rel: Mentions John the Baptist, "James, the brother of Jesus," and Herod; gives context to the Gospels and Acts.

extras.name: Tacitus, Annals
extras.what: The Roman historian tells how Nero blamed the Christians for the fire of Rome (AD 64).
extras.rel: Says "Christus" was executed by Pontius Pilate under Tiberius; background for the letters from Rome.

extras.name: Pliny the Younger, letter to Trajan
extras.what: A Roman governor in Turkey asks how to try Christians, who sing "to Christ as to a god."
extras.rel: Shows the pressure of the imperial cult in Asia Minor, the region of the seven churches of Revelation.

extras.name: Didache
extras.what: A short manual of Christian teaching: the "two ways," baptism, the Lord's Supper and leaders.
extras.rel: Shows how the churches receiving Paul's and Peter's letters lived.
extras.canon: Non-canonical; highly valued by early Christians.

extras.name: Gospel of Thomas
extras.what: A collection of 114 sayings attributed to Jesus, found complete in Coptic at Nag Hammadi (Egypt, 1945).
extras.rel: Some sayings resemble those in Matthew and Luke; others reflect later ideas. It does not narrate the death or resurrection.

extras.name: Protoevangelium of James
extras.what: An account of Mary's birth and childhood and of Jesus' birth in a cave.
extras.rel: The source of the traditional names of Mary's parents, Joachim and Anne.
extras.canon: Non-canonical; very influential in art and tradition.

extras.name: Shepherd of Hermas
extras.what: Visions and parables about repentance written in Rome.
extras.rel: It was included in Codex Sinaiticus alongside the New Testament; shows what churches read in the 2nd century.
extras.canon: Non-canonical; nearly entered the canon in some regions.

glossary.definition: "Look" or "pay attention": introduces something important.
The first son; he received a double inheritance and family leadership.
The firstborn's right to the main inheritance; Esau sold his to Jacob.
A solemn agreement with promises and commitments; in the Bible, between God and his people.
A sacrifice in which the animal was completely burned on the altar as an offering to God.
The act of covering or removing sin to restore the relationship with God.
The gold cover of the ark of the covenant, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement.
A portable tent that served as Israel's sanctuary in the wilderness.
A gold-covered wooden chest that held the tablets of the Law.
A vest-like priestly garment; sometimes also an object used to consult God.
Household idols, figures of family gods.
A sacred pole or tree dedicated to the false goddess asherah.
Hilltop altars, often used to worship false gods.
A member of the tribe of Levi, set apart to serve at the tabernacle and temple.
A person consecrated to God by a vow: no cutting the hair and no wine.
The chief priest; only he entered the Most Holy Place once a year.
Food God gave Israel in the wilderness; its name means "what is it?"
Every 50 years: slaves were freed and land returned to its families.
A tenth of harvests or income, given to God.
The first produce of the harvest, offered to God.
Removal of the foreskin; sign of God's covenant with Abraham.
Lacking the covenant sign; used for foreigners, such as the Philistines.
A person who speaks for God, often to warn and call to repentance.
An old name for a prophet.
In the book of Judges, a military and civil leader God raised up to rescue Israel.
Someone consecrated with oil for a task (king, priest); "messiah" in Hebrew, "christ" in Greek.
"Anointed one": the promised king from David's line.
A unit of weight (about 11 grams) also used as silver currency.
A very large unit of weight, about 34 kilograms of gold or silver.
A unit of length: elbow to fingertip, about 45 centimeters.
A Roman silver coin; a day's wage.
A dry measure for grain, about 22 liters.
A Jewish group devoted to careful keeping of the Law and traditions.
A group of the priestly elite; they did not believe in the resurrection.
A tax collector for Rome, seen as a traitor by fellow Jews.
An expert in copying and explaining the Scriptures.
The supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem.
A person from Samaria, of mixed descent; Jews and Samaritans rejected each other.
A person who is not Jewish.
"Good news": the message about Jesus.
"One who is sent": one of the Twelve or an authorized messenger like Paul.
A simple story that teaches a spiritual truth.
God's undeserved favor.
Being declared righteous before God.
Being set apart for God and gradually transformed.
Rescue by paying a price, like freeing a slave.
How the BSB renders God's name YHWH (often printed LORD in small capitals).
The place of the dead in the Old Testament.
A heavenly being guarding God's presence; cherub figures stood on the ark.
"Worthless": used for wicked people and, in the New Testament, for Satan.
A false god to whom children were sacrificed; the Bible strictly forbids it.
The Canaanite false god of storm; his name means "lord."
An image or figure worshiped as a god.
Going without food for a time to seek God.
Rough cloth worn as a sign of mourning or repentance.
The feast remembering the exodus; the angel "passed over" homes marked with blood.
Harvest feast 50 days after Passover; in Acts 2 the Holy Spirit comes.

parallels.title: Creation
parallels.note: Genesis narrates it; Psalm 104 sings it; John 1 rereads it in light of Christ.

parallels.title: The flood
parallels.note: Peter uses the flood as an image of baptism and of final judgment.

parallels.title: From Adam to Abraham
parallels.note: Chronicles summarizes the list and Luke carries it to Jesus.

parallels.title: Abraham's call
parallels.note: Stephen and Hebrews recall Abraham's faith in leaving without knowing where he was going.

parallels.title: The exodus
parallels.note: The psalms retell the exodus to teach new generations.

parallels.title: The Ten Commandments
parallels.note: Deuteronomy repeats them 40 years later; the reason for the Sabbath shifts from creation to liberation.

parallels.title: The golden calf
parallels.note: Moses recalls it as a warning; Stephen cites it in his defense.

parallels.title: The spies and Kadesh
parallels.note: Hebrews uses the unbelief at Kadesh as a warning to believers.

parallels.title: Balaam
parallels.note: The New Testament remembers him as the example of a teacher who sells out.

parallels.title: baal of Peor
parallels.note: Paul uses it to warn Corinth against idolatry and immorality.

parallels.title: David and Goliath
parallels.note: A Qumran manuscript gives Goliath a different height; Psalm 151 sings of it.

parallels.title: Saul's death
parallels.note: Three versions: the battle, the Amalekite's report and Chronicles' summary.

parallels.title: David takes Jerusalem
parallels.note: The Tel Dan Stele mentions the "house of David" a century later.

parallels.title: The ark comes to Jerusalem
parallels.note: Chronicles adds the songs and the organization of the Levites.

parallels.title: The promise to David
parallels.note: Psalm 89 sings it and Luke 1 applies it to Jesus.

parallels.title: David and Bathsheba
parallels.note: Psalm 51 is David's prayer after Nathan confronted him.

parallels.title: Absalom's rebellion
parallels.note: The title of Psalm 3 places it during David's flight.

parallels.title: Solomon's temple
parallels.note: Two accounts of the building and dedication.

parallels.title: The kingdom divides
parallels.note: Kings follows both kingdoms; Chronicles stays with Judah.

parallels.title: Elijah against baal
parallels.note: Jesus and James recall the drought and Elijah's prayer.

parallels.title: Moab's revolt
parallels.note: King Mesha told his own version on the Mesha Stele.

parallels.title: Jehu's revolt
parallels.note: Hosea condemns the blood shed at Jezreel.

parallels.title: The fall of Samaria
parallels.note: Kings tells it twice and explains why it happened.

parallels.title: Sennacherib besieges Jerusalem
parallels.note: Three nearly identical biblical accounts and the Assyrian version on Sennacherib's Prism.

parallels.title: Manasseh's reign
parallels.note: Chronicles adds his repentance in Babylon; tradition blames him for Isaiah's death.

parallels.title: Josiah's reform
parallels.note: Both tell of finding the Book of the Law and destroying the altars to false gods.

parallels.title: The destruction of Jerusalem
parallels.note: Four accounts and a whole book of lament; the Babylonian Chronicles and Lachish letters confirm it.

parallels.title: Cyrus's decree
parallels.note: Isaiah announces it, Chronicles ends with it and Ezra begins with it.

parallels.title: Jonah and Nineveh
parallels.note: Jesus uses Jonah as a sign of his death and resurrection.

parallels.title: The birth of Jesus
parallels.note: Matthew tells it from Joseph and the magi; Luke from Mary and the shepherds.

parallels.title: Jesus' baptism
parallels.note: All four Gospels tell it; Josephus also writes about John the Baptist.

parallels.title: The Sermon on the Mount
parallels.note: Luke has a shorter version "on a level place."

parallels.title: Feeding of the five thousand
parallels.note: The only miracle besides the resurrection told in all four Gospels.

parallels.title: The calling of Matthew (Levi)
parallels.note: Mark and Luke call him Levi; Matthew uses his other name. Afterward Jesus eats with tax collectors.

parallels.title: The transfiguration
parallels.note: Peter recalls it as an eyewitness.

parallels.title: The Last Supper
parallels.note: Paul passes on Jesus' words about 20 years later.

parallels.title: Jesus' death and resurrection
parallels.note: Four Gospels, Paul's summary, and mentions in Tacitus and Josephus.

parallels.title: Paul's conversion
parallels.note: Acts tells it three times and Paul summarizes it in Galatians.

parallels.title: The Jerusalem council
parallels.note: Luke and Paul tell of the meeting from different angles.

parallels.title: Ephesus and artemis
parallels.note: The riot in Ephesus, the letter to that church and the message of Revelation 2.

art.title: The Creation of Adam
art.note: Fresco on the Sistine Chapel ceiling in the Vatican. God reaches out to give life to the first man.

art.title: The Expulsion from the Garden of Eden
art.article: Expulsion from the Garden of Eden
art.note: Fresco in the Brancacci Chapel, Florence. One of the first paintings to show human grief so realistically.

art.title: Expulsion from the Garden of Eden
art.article: Expulsion from the Garden of Eden (Cole)
art.note: A contrast between the bright paradise and the wild world Adam and Eve enter.

art.title: The Tower of Babel
art.note: Bruegel imagined it like the Roman Colosseum. Mesopotamian ziggurats inspired the story.

art.title: Abraham and the Three Angels
art.note: Abraham welcomes three visitors at Mamre; they announce that Sarah will have a son.

art.title: The Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah
art.article: The Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah
art.note: Lot and his daughters flee as fire falls from the sky.

art.title: The Sacrifice of Isaac
art.note: The angel stops Abraham's hand at the last moment; beside them, the ram that takes Isaac's place.

art.title: Joseph Recognized by His Brothers
art.note: Joseph, now governor of Egypt, reveals himself to the brothers who sold him.

art.title: The Finding of Moses
art.note: Pharaoh's daughter carries the baby rescued from the Nile, in an Egypt rebuilt with archaeological detail.

art.title: The Seventh Plague of Egypt
art.note: Hail and fire fall on Egypt as Moses stretches out his arms.

art.title: The Crossing of the Red Sea
art.article: The Crossing of the Red Sea (Poussin)
art.note: The Israelites are safe as the sea closes over the Egyptian army.

art.title: The Adoration of the Golden Calf
art.article: The Adoration of the Golden Calf
art.note: The people dance before the false god; in the background Moses comes down the mountain with the tablets.

art.title: Moses
art.note: Sculpture in San Pietro in Vincoli, Rome. The "horns" come from a Latin translation of Exodus 34:29, where his face "shone."

art.title: Balaam and the Donkey
art.note: The donkey sees the angel Balaam cannot, and refuses to move on.

art.title: Samson and Delilah
art.note: Samson sleeps while his hair is cut; the Philistines wait outside.

art.title: David
art.note: A 5-meter sculpture in Florence: David focused just before facing Goliath.

art.title: David with the Head of Goliath
art.article: David with the Head of Goliath (Caravaggio, Rome)
art.note: Caravaggio painted his own face on Goliath's head.

art.title: Bathsheba with King David's Letter
art.note: Bathsheba holds David's letter; her gaze anticipates the tragedy that follows.

art.title: The Judgement of Solomon
art.note: Solomon orders the child divided to reveal the true mother.

art.title: Elijah in the Desert
art.note: Elijah, exhausted after facing baal's prophets, receives bread from the angel.

art.title: Jeremiah Lamenting the Destruction of Jerusalem
art.article: Jeremiah Lamenting the Destruction of Jerusalem
art.note: The prophet broods as Jerusalem burns in the background.

art.title: Belshazzar's Feast
art.note: A hand writes on the wall as the king drinks from the Jerusalem temple's vessels.

art.title: Belshazzar's Feast
art.note: Babylon imagined as a colossal city on the night it falls.

art.title: Daniel in the Lions' Den
art.note: Rubens studied real lions to paint this picture.

art.title: The Ancient of Days
art.note: The title comes from Daniel 7; Blake painted him measuring the world with a compass.

art.title: The Annunciation
art.note: One of Leonardo's earliest works: the angel Gabriel greets Mary.

art.title: Mystic Nativity
art.note: Angels dance above the stable as the shepherds come to worship.

art.title: Adoration of the Magi
art.note: Botticelli cast the Medici family as the magi; he appears himself on the right.

art.title: Christ in the House of His Parents
art.article: Christ in the House of His Parents
art.note: The boy Jesus in Joseph's workshop; a wound on his hand foreshadows the cross.

art.title: The Baptism of Christ
art.article: The Baptism of Christ (Verrocchio and Leonardo)
art.note: The young Leonardo painted the angel on the left in his master's workshop.
art.credit: Photo: Andrea del Verrocchio / Leonardo da Vinci · CC BY-SA 4.0

art.title: Salome with the Head of John the Baptist
art.article: Salome with the Head of John the Baptist (Caravaggio, London)
art.note: Herod has John beheaded to keep his promise to Salome.

art.title: The Calling of Saint Matthew
art.note: Jesus points to the tax collector; the light enters along with the call.

art.title: The Feast in the House of Levi
art.article: The Feast in the House of Levi
art.note: It was meant to be a "Last Supper," but the Inquisition objected to its details and Veronese changed the title.

art.title: The Storm on the Sea of Galilee
art.article: The Storm on the Sea of Galilee
art.note: His only seascape. It was stolen in Boston in 1990 and is still missing.

art.title: The Wedding at Cana
art.note: Jesus' first miracle in John's Gospel: water turned into wine.

art.title: The Tribute Money
art.note: Peter finds the tax coin in a fish's mouth.

art.title: Christ and the Woman Taken in Adultery
art.article: Christ and the Woman Taken in Adultery (Bruegel)
art.note: Jesus writes on the ground: "Let any one of you who is without sin…"

art.title: The Return of the Prodigal Son
art.article: The Return of the Prodigal Son (Rembrandt)
art.note: Painted near the end of his life; the father's hands differ: one strong, one tender.

art.title: The Raising of Lazarus
art.article: The Raising of Lazarus (Sebastiano del Piombo)
art.note: Michelangelo helped with the drawings of Lazarus.

art.title: The Raising of Lazarus
art.note: Jesus raises his hand and Lazarus rises from the tomb.

art.title: The Transfiguration
art.note: His last work. Above, Jesus with Moses and Elijah; below, the possessed boy (Matthew 17:14).

art.title: The Last Supper
art.note: A mural in Milan. It captures the moment Jesus says "one of you will betray me": the apostles react in groups of three and Judas leans back.

art.title: The Agony in the Garden
art.note: Jesus prays while the disciples sleep and Judas approaches with the soldiers.

art.title: The Taking of Christ
art.note: Judas's kiss. It was lost until 1990, in a Jesuit house in Dublin.

art.title: The Denial of Saint Peter
art.note: The servant girl points at Peter, who denies knowing Jesus.

art.title: Christ Carrying the Cross
art.note: Grotesque faces surround Jesus, calm in the middle of the crowd.

art.title: Christ Crucified
art.note: Prado Museum. Above the cross, the sign in Hebrew, Greek and Latin (John 19:20).

art.title: Isenheim Altarpiece
art.note: Made for a hospital: Christ is shown with sores like those of the sick who looked at him.

art.title: Pietà
art.note: Mary holds Jesus' body. It is the only work Michelangelo signed.
art.credit: Photo: original file by Stanislav Traykov · CC BY 2.5

art.title: Lamentation of Christ
art.note: A bold view from the feet; the nail wounds are visible.

art.title: The Entombment of Christ
art.note: Nicodemus and John lower the body into the tomb (John 19:39).

art.title: The Resurrection
art.note: Jesus rises from the tomb while the guards sleep.

art.title: Noli me tangere
art.note: "Do not hold on to me": the risen Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene.

art.title: The Incredulity of Saint Thomas
art.note: Thomas puts his finger into the wound in Jesus' side (John 20:27).

art.title: Supper at Emmaus
art.note: The moment the disciples recognize Jesus as he breaks the bread.

art.title: The Liberation of Saint Peter
art.note: Vatican fresco: the angel leads Peter out of Herod's prison.

art.title: The Conversion of Saint Paul
art.note: Saul falls from his horse, blinded by the light, on the road to Damascus.

art.title: The Crucifixion of Saint Peter
art.note: Tradition says Peter asked to be crucified upside down; Jesus foretells it in John 21:18.

art.title: The Great Day of His Wrath
art.article: The Great Day of His Wrath
art.note: Inspired by Revelation 6:17: mountains and cities collapse.

art.title: The Last Judgment
art.note: The altar wall of the Sistine Chapel, with more than 300 figures.

films.title: Cabiria
films.note: An Italian epic about Carthage during the Punic Wars. It inspired Griffith and DeMille, and it is cinema's best recreation of the Carthaginian cult of baal hammon, which the film calls moloch.

fragments.title: The temple of moloch
fragments.note: Priests offer children to the statue's fire. The Bible forbids and condemns this practice: Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2–5, Jeremiah 7:31, and Josiah destroys the altar at Topheth (2 Kings 23:10). An intense scene, though nothing graphic is shown.

films.title: The Ten Commandments
films.note: The biblical prologue (the first 50 minutes) recreates the Exodus, with intertitles taken from the Bible. The rest is a modern story.

fragments.title: Moses before Pharaoh
fragments.note: "Let my people go": Moses confronts Pharaoh after nine plagues.

fragments.title: The death of the firstborn
fragments.note: The tenth plague and the departure from Egypt (Exodus 12:29–32).

fragments.title: The crossing of the Red Sea
fragments.note: The sea parts, Israel crosses and the water covers Pharaoh's chariots. One of the most famous special effects of silent film.

fragments.title: Sinai and the golden calf
fragments.note: The commandments appear in the sky while the people worship the golden calf at the foot of the mountain.

films.title: The King of Kings
films.note: The life of Jesus according to the Gospels, with Bible quotes in the intertitles. The resurrection is in color (two-strip Technicolor).

fragments.title: Mary Magdalene meets Jesus
fragments.note: The film imagines the encounter in which Jesus drives seven demons out of Mary (Luke 8:2).

fragments.title: Jesus' miracles
fragments.note: Healings and the girl brought back to life.

fragments.title: The entry into Jerusalem
fragments.note: "Hosanna in the highest!" (Mark 11:10).

fragments.title: The Last Supper
fragments.note: "Take, eat; this is my body" (Luke 22:19). The composition imitates Leonardo's mural.

fragments.title: Gethsemane and the arrest
fragments.note: Jesus prays in the garden and Judas arrives with the soldiers.

fragments.title: Jesus before Pilate
fragments.note: The trial and the crowd calling for Barabbas.

fragments.title: The crucifixion
fragments.note: Calvary, the earthquake and the darkness (Matthew 27:45–54).

fragments.title: The resurrection
fragments.note: In color: the empty tomb and Jesus with his disciples.

films.title: From the Manger to the Cross
films.note: The first film about Jesus shot in Egypt and the Holy Land: the landscapes are real. It is on the U.S. National Film Registry.

fragments.title: The birth and the magi
fragments.note: The manger, the shepherds and the magi, with quotes from Matthew and Luke in the intertitles.

fragments.title: The flight into Egypt
fragments.note: Filmed in front of the pyramids of Giza.

fragments.title: Jesus calls his disciples
fragments.note: Peter, Andrew, James and John by the Sea of Galilee.

fragments.title: The anointing at Bethany and Judas
fragments.note: A woman pours perfume on Jesus; Judas goes to the priests.

fragments.title: The Last Supper and the crucifixion
fragments.note: From the supper to Calvary.

films.title: Noah's Ark
films.note: It mixes a World War I story with the flood narrative. Real injuries happened while filming the flood because of the amount of water used.

fragments.title: The tower of Babel
fragments.note: A short prologue: people build a tower "whose top reaches heaven."

fragments.title: The flood
fragments.note: The flood falls on the idolatrous city while the ark floats. The film invents characters who are not in Genesis.

films.title: Intolerance
films.note: Four interwoven stories. The Babylon story recreates the city's fall to Cyrus (539 BC) on gigantic sets; the Judean story shows Jesus at Cana, with the adulterous woman and on the cross.

fragments.title: Babylon and Cyrus (throughout the film)
fragments.note: The Babylon scenes are intercut with the other stories. It shows Belshazzar and the worship of marduk and ishtar.

films.title: Ben-Hur
films.note: From Lew Wallace's novel. It opens with the birth in Bethlehem (in color), and Judah Ben-Hur's life crosses with Jesus' until the crucifixion.

fragments.title: Bethlehem and the life of Jesus (throughout the film)
fragments.note: Historical fiction: Jesus appears in brief moments, almost always without showing his face.

films.title: Judith of Bethulia
films.note: Griffith's first feature film, based on the book of Judith (deuterocanonical).

fragments.title: Judith and Holofernes
fragments.note: The widow who saves her city from the Assyrian army.

films.title: Salomé
films.note: Based on Oscar Wilde's play, with art deco design. It embellishes the story: the Gospels don't name Herodias's daughter.

fragments.title: Herod and John the Baptist
fragments.note: The death of John the Baptist; Josephus gives Salome's name.
